chapter.name: The Price Puzzle: What Drives the Market
chapter.blurb: Demand and supply, their laws and determinants, market equilibrium, dynamic markets and the role and limits of government.

scope_in.item: Demand, the law of demand, individual and market demand
Factors affecting demand: related goods, income, taste, population, marginal utility, seasons, expectations
Supply, law of supply, market supply and factors affecting supply
Market equilibrium, excess demand and excess supply
Dynamic markets: why equilibrium keeps changing; hotel tariffs and face masks
Role of government: regulation, price ceilings and floors, monopolies, public goods and limits of intervention

scope_out.item: Detailed market structures such as oligopoly
Money, banking and inflation in detail

scope_out.reason: Only tables and graphs are used

concepts.name: Demand, the law of demand and the demand curve
concepts.description: The meaning of demand, the law of demand, individual and market demand schedules and demand curves.
concepts.idea: Demand is the willingness and ability to buy; as price rises the quantity demanded falls.
concepts.rule: Demand: the quantity people are willing and able to buy at a price. Law of Demand: inverse relationship between price and quantity demanded. Individual demand is shown by a demand schedule and a downward-sloping demand curve. Market demand is the sum of all individual demands.
concepts.example: Srivalli buys 1 kg of mangoes at Rs 150, 2 kg at Rs 100 and 3 kg at Rs 50.

questions.q: Demand for a product is
questions.a: the quantity people are willing and able to buy at a particular price
o: the quantity people are willing and able to buy at a particular price

questions.q: The Law of Demand shows
questions.a: an inverse relationship between price and quantity demanded
o: an inverse relationship between price and quantity demanded
a direct relationship between price and quantity demanded

questions.q: A demand schedule, drawn as a graph, gives the demand ____.
questions.a: curve

questions.q: Market demand is
questions.a: the sum of all individual demands
o: the sum of all individual demands

questions.q: When the price of a product rises, the quantity demanded generally
questions.a: decreases

questions.q: Demand is not just desire but
questions.a: willingness complemented by the ability or purchasing power to buy
o: willingness complemented by the ability or purchasing power to buy

questions.q: The individual demand curve slopes
questions.a: downward

questions.q: The market demand curve is flatter than an individual curve because
questions.a: many consumers together respond more strongly to a price change
o: many consumers together respond more strongly to a price change

questions.q: Explain the Law of Demand using the mango example.
questions.a: At Rs 150 per kg Srivalli buys 1 kg, at Rs 100 she buys 2 kg and at Rs 50 she buys 3 kg. As the price falls the quantity demanded rises, an inverse relationship.
s: Uses the price and quantity numbers
Says price falls and quantity demanded rises

questions.q: Srivalli buys how many kg of mangoes at Rs 100 per kg?
questions.a: 2 kg

questions.q: At Rs 50 per kg Srivalli buys ____ kg of mangoes.
When the price fell from Rs 150 to Rs 50, Srivalli's demand rose by
questions.a: 2 kg

questions.q: Draw up the demand schedule for Srivalli and identify the points on the demand curve.
questions.a: Price 150: 1 kg (point A); price 100: 2 kg (point B); price 50: 3 kg (point C). Joining A, B and C gives the downward-sloping line DD.
s: Points A, B, C and the downward curve

questions.q: What assumption is made when drawing an individual demand curve?
questions.a: Other factors such as income and taste are assumed to be constant, so only price and quantity demanded change.

questions.q: Explain how individual demand is added to get market demand and what the market demand curve looks like.
questions.a: Market demand at each price is the sum of the demands of all consumers (Q1 + Q2 + Q3). Plotting these totals gives the market demand curve, which also slopes downward and is flatter than an individual curve.
s: Summing individual demands at each price

questions.q: Which statement about demand is correct?
questions.a: A person who wants a car but cannot pay for it has no demand for it
o: A person who wants a car but cannot pay for it has no demand for it
Everyone who wants a product has demand for it
Demand is the same as supply

questions.q: Why is willingness alone not enough to constitute demand?
questions.a: Demand also needs the ability or purchasing power to buy; without money the desire cannot become effective demand in the market.

questions.q: Explain why market demand changes more than individual demand for the same fall in price.
questions.a: Market demand aggregates many consumers, so the same price change leads to a larger total quantity response. When price fell from Rs 150 to Rs 50 Srivalli's demand rose by 2 kg but market demand rose by 12 kg.
s: The example numbers 2 kg and 12 kg

questions.q: Ravi says when the price of a product falls, people always buy less. Evaluate.
questions.a: He is wrong. By the Law of Demand, a fall in price generally raises the quantity demanded.

questions.q: Make your own demand schedule for notebooks at three prices and say at what price you would stop buying.
questions.a: For example: Rs 20: buy 5; Rs 40: buy 3; Rs 80: buy 1; Rs 120: buy 0. I stop buying when a notebook is too costly for my pocket money.
s: Price at which buying stops with a reason

concepts.name: Factors that influence demand
concepts.description: Substitute and complementary goods, income, tastes, population, diminishing marginal utility, seasons and expectations.
concepts.idea: Demand can change even when the price stays the same.
concepts.rule: Substitute goods replace each other (tea and coffee); complementary goods are used together (printer and cartridge). Rising income raises demand. Diminishing marginal utility: additional satisfaction falls as more is consumed. Seasons and expectations of future prices also change demand.
concepts.example: People delay buying durables before Diwali expecting discounts, which decreases present demand.

questions.q: Goods that can replace each other, like tea and coffee, are
questions.a: substitute goods

questions.q: Goods used together, like cars and petrol, are
questions.a: complementary goods

questions.q: When household income rises, the demand for several goods generally ____.
questions.a: rises

questions.q: The principle that additional usefulness falls as more of a good is consumed is
questions.a: diminishing marginal utility

questions.q: If the price of coffee rises, the demand for tea
questions.a: may rise

questions.q: If movie tickets become more expensive, demand for popcorn sold in cinemas
questions.a: may fall

questions.q: More children in a population generally increases demand for
questions.a: sports shoes

questions.q: If consumers expect prices to fall in future, current demand
questions.a: decreases as they postpone purchases

questions.q: What is diminishing marginal utility? Explain with mangoes.
questions.a: The additional usefulness from a good falls as more of it is consumed. The first mango is delicious but by the third or fourth you are barely interested, so willingness to pay and demand fall.

questions.q: A rise in the price of a substitute usually
questions.a: increases demand for the other good
o: increases demand for the other good
decreases demand for the other good

questions.q: If demand for printers rises, demand for printer ____ may also rise.
questions.a: cartridges

questions.q: Sweaters being in demand in winter is an example of
questions.a: seasonal demand

questions.q: Give one example each of substitute and complementary goods from the chapter.
questions.a: Substitutes: tea and coffee (or mangoes and bananas). Complements: smartphones and earphones, cars and petrol, or printers and cartridges.

questions.q: Why did Srivalli not buy oranges instead of mangoes even when they were cheaper?
questions.a: Her taste and preference for mangoes meant she could not substitute them with oranges.
s: Not substituting even at a lower price

questions.q: Explain how income, taste and future expectations affect demand with examples.
questions.a: Higher income lets people buy more or better goods. Tastes decide preferences, like liking mangoes over oranges. If people expect prices to fall, as before Diwali or the New Year, they postpone buying and present demand falls.

questions.q: India's large population influences demand by
questions.a: contributing strongly to consumer demand and economic growth
o: contributing strongly to consumer demand and economic growth

questions.q: Does an increase in income always increase demand for all goods? Defend or refute.
questions.a: Not always. It generally raises demand for many goods, but consumers may choose higher-quality alternatives, so demand for some cheaper goods may not rise. Other factors such as taste also matter.
s: Not for every good; other factors matter

questions.q: Explain why demand may change even when the price of a good remains the same.
questions.a: Because of changes in prices of related goods, income, taste, population size and composition, seasons and festivals, and expectations of future prices. For instance a new smartphone model sees a rush even at a high price.

questions.q: Tara says demand depends only on price. Evaluate.
questions.a: She is wrong. Demand also depends on prices of related goods, income, tastes, population, seasons and expectations, as the chapter shows.

questions.q: Ask a family member if they postponed or advanced buying a product because of expected price changes and explain how it fits the chapter.
questions.a: For example a family delayed buying a television before Diwali expecting a festival discount; this shows how future price expectations reduce present demand.

concepts.name: Supply, the law of supply and factors affecting supply
concepts.description: The meaning of supply, the law of supply, market supply and the factors that change supply.
concepts.idea: As price rises, sellers offer more; other factors can shift supply too.
concepts.rule: Supply is the quantity sellers are willing and able to offer at a price. Law of supply: as price rises quantity supplied rises. Market supply is the sum of individual supplies. Supply depends on the price, prices of related goods, number of sellers, technology, input costs, expectations and weather.
concepts.example: A farmer who sees high chickpea prices and low wheat prices will grow more chickpeas next season.

questions.q: Supply is the quantity of a product that sellers are
questions.a: willing and able to offer at a particular price
o: willing and able to offer at a particular price

questions.q: The law of supply says that as price rises, quantity supplied
questions.a: increases

questions.q: The supply curve slopes ____.
questions.a: upward

questions.q: Market supply is
questions.a: the sum of all individual supplies
o: the sum of all individual supplies

questions.q: Higher prices increase quantity supplied because
questions.a: they increase profitability and attract new firms
o: they increase profitability and attract new firms

questions.q: At the start of the mango season, supply is low so mangoes are
questions.a: costly

questions.q: Improved technology such as drip irrigation generally
questions.a: raises supply by reducing costs and raising output
o: raises supply by reducing costs and raising output

questions.q: More sellers in a market means
questions.a: higher competition and greater market supply, so prices tend to fall
o: higher competition and greater market supply, so prices tend to fall

questions.q: Explain the law of supply.
questions.a: As price increases, sellers supply more because higher prices bring more profit, and new firms enter; as price falls, quantity supplied falls.
s: Direct relationship between price and quantity supplied
Reason such as profit and new firms

questions.q: A seller supplies 2 kg of mangoes at Rs 100 and 3 kg at Rs 150. This shows
questions.a: an upward-sloping supply curve

questions.q: Supply is low and prices are high at the start of the mango ____.
questions.a: season

questions.q: If wheat prices are low but chickpea prices are high, a farmer will
questions.a: grow more chickpeas

questions.q: Name two factors that affect supply.
questions.a: The price of the good, prices of related goods, number of sellers, technology, input costs, expectations and weather.

questions.q: How does cold storage in transporting mangoes change supply?
questions.a: It lets mangoes reach distant markets without spoiling, increasing the quantity supplied in the market.
s: Reduces spoilage and reaches distant markets

questions.q: Explain the effect of technology, expectations and number of sellers on supply with examples.
questions.a: Technology like drip irrigation lowers cost and raises supply. If potato wholesalers expect higher prices, they hold back supply now. More sellers raise supply and competition, lowering price.

questions.q: If supply is less than demand, prices
questions.a: rise

questions.q: Why might potato wholesalers hold back supply now?
questions.a: If they expect prices to rise in the peak season, they can sell later at higher prices, so present supply falls.

questions.q: Explain how prices depend on the interaction between demand and supply during the mango season.
questions.a: At the start supply is low, so mangoes are costly and people buy little. As supply increases mid-season, prices fall and demand rises. When supply is below demand prices rise; when supply exceeds demand prices fall.
s: Early season low supply and high price
Mid-season more supply and lower price

questions.q: Sam says sellers supply more when prices fall. Evaluate.
questions.a: He is wrong. By the law of supply sellers supply less when prices fall because profits are lower.

questions.q: A farmer installs drip irrigation, cutting water use by 40 per cent and raising yield by 30 per cent. Explain the effect on his supply and on market supply if many adopt it.
questions.a: His cost per unit falls and output rises, so he is willing to supply more at each price. If many farmers adopt it, market supply increases and prices tend to fall.
s: More willing to supply at each price
Market supply rises and prices tend to fall

concepts.name: Market equilibrium and price determination
concepts.description: How prices are determined by demand and supply, excess demand and excess supply, and the equilibrium price and quantity.
concepts.idea: Price settles where the quantity demanded equals the quantity supplied.
concepts.rule: At a low price there is excess demand (shortage); at a high price there is excess supply (surplus). At the market equilibrium quantity demanded equals quantity supplied, and the market clears. In the mango example the equilibrium price is Rs 100 and the equilibrium quantity 12 kg.
concepts.example: At Rs 100 per kg, both demand and supply are 12 kg, so there is no pressure on the price to change.

questions.q: Prices are determined by
questions.a: the interaction of demand and supply
o: the interaction of demand and supply

questions.q: Market equilibrium occurs when
questions.a: quantity demanded equals quantity supplied

questions.q: The equilibrium price of mangoes in the example is Rs ____ per kg.
The equilibrium quantity in the example is
questions.a: 12 kg

questions.q: At a price lower than the equilibrium price there is
questions.a: excess demand

questions.q: At a price higher than the equilibrium price there is
questions.a: excess supply

questions.q: At equilibrium the market is said to be "cleared" because
questions.a: there is neither a shortage nor a surplus
o: there is neither a shortage nor a surplus
price is fixed by the government

questions.q: On the graph, equilibrium is at
questions.a: the point where the demand and supply curves intersect
o: the point where the demand and supply curves intersect

questions.q: Explain excess demand and excess supply.
questions.a: Excess demand is when quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied, usually at a low price. Excess supply is when quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded, usually at a high price.

questions.q: If mangoes sell at Rs 40 per kg where demand is much higher than supply, there is
questions.a: excess demand

questions.q: At the equilibrium price of Rs 100 the quantity demanded and supplied are both ____ kg.
When there is excess demand, the price tends to
questions.a: rise

questions.q: What happens to price when there is excess supply, and why?
questions.a: The price falls, because sellers have unsold goods and lower prices attract buyers until quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.
s: Reason: unsold stock and lower price attracting buyers

questions.q: State the equilibrium price and quantity in the mango example and what they mean.
questions.a: Equilibrium price Rs 100 and equilibrium quantity 12 kg. At this point there is no shortage or surplus and no pressure for price to change.
s: No shortage, surplus or pressure to change

questions.q: Describe how a market moves to equilibrium from a price that is too low and one that is too high.
questions.a: At a low price, excess demand creates a shortage; buyers compete and price rises. At a high price, excess supply leaves unsold goods; sellers cut prices. The price moves until quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.

questions.q: A market that is "cleared" has
questions.a: no pressure for prices to change
o: no pressure for prices to change

questions.q: Why does price rise when demand exceeds supply?
questions.a: Buyers compete for the limited goods and are willing to pay more, and sellers can charge more, so price rises until supply meets demand.

questions.q: Using the equilibrium idea, explain why sellers cut prices at online festival sales.
questions.a: Sellers with unsold stock (excess supply) lower prices to attract buyers and clear stocks; lower prices raise quantity demanded, moving towards a new equilibrium at a lower price. Consumers gain lower prices and sellers gain volume and stock clearance.
s: Benefits to both consumers and sellers

questions.q: Meera says equilibrium price is fixed by the government. Evaluate.
questions.a: She is wrong. In a market, equilibrium is found where demand and supply meet; the government does not set it unless it intervenes.
s: Says equilibrium is set by demand and supply

questions.q: Plot the demand and supply of mangoes at Rs 40, Rs 100 and Rs 150 and describe where excess demand and excess supply appear.
questions.a: At Rs 40 quantity demanded exceeds supplied, giving excess demand; at Rs 100 they are equal at 12 kg, the equilibrium; at Rs 150 supplied exceeds demanded, giving excess supply.

concepts.name: Dynamic markets: does equilibrium exist in the real world?
concepts.description: Why real-world equilibrium keeps moving, with examples such as face masks in 2020 and hotel tariffs.
concepts.idea: Real markets keep changing, so equilibrium is never fully stable.
concepts.rule: Changes in technology, wages, interest rates, wars, pandemics, weather and disasters alter demand and supply, so the market keeps adjusting to a new equilibrium. Hotel tariffs vary with demand, season and events.
concepts.example: During the 2020 pandemic demand for face masks surged and prices rose before supply adjusted.

questions.q: In the real world, market equilibrium is
questions.a: never stable and moves all the time
o: never stable and moves all the time

questions.q: During the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020, the demand for face masks
questions.a: surged rapidly

questions.q: Markets are called ____ because prices keep changing with conditions.
questions.a: dynamic

questions.q: Hotel room prices are also called
questions.a: tariffs

questions.q: When demand for masks surged, the supply
questions.a: could not catch up immediately and price rose significantly
o: could not catch up immediately and price rose significantly

questions.q: Which of these can change demand and supply in the real world?
questions.a: technology, wages, interest rates, wars, pandemics and weather
o: technology, wages, interest rates, wars, pandemics and weather

questions.q: A hotel may cut the tariff by 40 per cent overnight when
questions.a: a group tour cancels its booking
o: a group tour cancels its booking

questions.q: Hotels charge different tariffs on New Year's Eve because
questions.a: demand is very high

questions.q: Why is real-world equilibrium never fully stable?
questions.a: Conditions such as technology, wages, wars, pandemics, weather and disasters constantly change demand and supply, so the market is always adjusting to a new equilibrium.

questions.q: After the pandemic passed, the prices of masks
questions.a: fell as demand reduced

questions.q: A hotel in Goa may charge Rs 25,000 on ____ Eve because demand is very high.
questions.a: New Year's

questions.q: A hotel changing its tariff several times a day is doing so to
questions.a: earn maximum revenue as demand changes
o: earn maximum revenue as demand changes

questions.q: Name two factors that influence hotel tariffs.
questions.a: How fast rooms are being booked, tariffs of nearby hotels, festivals, conferences or events, and the number of days left before arrival.

questions.q: Explain how the price of masks changed from 2020 onwards.
questions.a: Demand surged so price rose sharply; over time suppliers increased output and prices fell; after the pandemic demand reduced and prices went back down.
s: Later fall as supply adjusted and demand fell

questions.q: Explain with the Goa hotel example how demand and season change prices.
questions.a: On an off-season weekday demand is low so tariff is low; on a December weekend in the tourist season it is Rs 8,000; on New Year's Eve with very high demand it is Rs 25,000 per night. Prices follow demand.

questions.q: Why should we think about long-term sustainability even when demand is high?
questions.a: High demand for fast fashion, overfishing and overuse of groundwater can harm future supply
o: High demand for fast fashion, overfishing and overuse of groundwater can harm future supply
Sustainability has no link with markets

questions.q: Give another real-life example besides hotels where prices change frequently and why.
questions.a: Airline tickets change price by day and season because demand and seats available change; vegetables are cheaper in the evening as sellers clear stock.
s: Reason related to demand or supply

questions.q: Explain why markets are described as dynamic systems rather than machines with fixed equilibria.
questions.a: They respond to changes in technology, income, weather, trends and events, so demand and supply keep shifting and the market is always adjusting to a new equilibrium, never fully settling at the old one.
s: Always adjusting to a new equilibrium

questions.q: Ali says once a market reaches equilibrium it stays there for ever. Evaluate.
questions.a: He is wrong. Changes in demand or supply, such as a pandemic or new technology, move the equilibrium, and the market adjusts to a new one.

questions.q: Visit a vegetable market and explain why tomato prices might be high in the morning and lower in the evening.
questions.a: In the morning fresh stock and demand are high so sellers charge more; by evening sellers want to clear unsold perishable tomatoes and cut prices, showing supply and demand at work.

concepts.name: The role and limits of government in the market
concepts.description: Why and how the government intervenes: regulation of unfair practices, price ceilings and floors, monopolies, regulators, essential commodities, public goods and the limitations of intervention.
concepts.idea: Markets do not always work fairly, so the government regulates and provides public goods, but too much intervention has costs.
concepts.rule: Price ceiling: maximum price (for example for medicines). Price floor: lower limit such as a minimum wage. Regulators: RBI, Central Consumer Protection Authority, TRAI, SEBI. Public goods (roads, defence, sanitation) are provided by the government. Limits: price distortions, heavy regulation, discouraged innovation.
concepts.example: In COVID-19 the government capped the retail price of a 200 ml sanitiser at Rs 100 under the Essential Commodities Act, 1955.

questions.q: A maximum price fixed by the government is called a
questions.a: price ceiling

questions.q: A minimum wage is an example of a
questions.a: price floor

questions.q: Roads, bridges and street lighting are examples of ____ goods.
questions.a: public

questions.q: Which body regulates the securities market in India?
questions.a: SEBI

questions.q: The government intervenes in markets because
questions.a: markets do not always work fairly, for example for essential goods like medicines
o: markets do not always work fairly, for example for essential goods like medicines

questions.q: A monopoly is harmful to consumers because it may
questions.a: charge higher prices, give poorer quality and restrict supply
o: charge higher prices, give poorer quality and restrict supply

questions.q: Public goods are usually not provided by private companies because they
questions.a: do not generate direct profit

questions.q: The RBI regulates
questions.a: banking

questions.q: Why does the government set a price ceiling on essential medicines?
questions.a: To prevent overcharging so that essential medicines remain accessible to all, including vulnerable and low-income groups.

questions.q: In COVID-19 the maximum retail price of a 200 ml sanitiser bottle was capped at
questions.a: Rs 100

questions.q: Sanitisers were declared essential commodities under the Essential Commodities Act of ____.
The Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) regulates
questions.a: telecommunications

questions.q: Name two regulators and the sector each regulates.
questions.a: RBI for banking; TRAI for telecommunications; SEBI for the securities market; Central Consumer Protection Authority for consumer rights and unfair trade practices.

questions.q: Why do goods like a neighbourhood park often need government provision?
questions.a: Everyone benefits but individuals may hope others pay, so not enough money is collected and the park is never built; government funding ensures such goods are provided.
s: Everyone benefits but some avoid paying
Government provision or funding ensures supply

questions.q: Explain the government's intervention during the sanitiser shortage of COVID-19 and its effects.
questions.a: Demand surged, causing stockouts, hoarding and black-marketing. The government declared sanitisers essential commodities under the Essential Commodities Act 1955 and capped the price at Rs 100 for 200 ml. Many companies began production and sanitisers became widely available at fair prices.

questions.q: If the government fixes the price of wheat at Rs 20 when the market price would be Rs 30, farmers may
questions.a: produce less, leading to shortages

questions.q: State two limitations of government intervention with examples.
questions.a: Price distortions: a low maximum price reduces producers' incentives and may cause shortages. Heavy regulation: licences and permits burden small enterprises like a small restaurant. It can also discourage innovation.

questions.q: Discuss how a democratic government should decide when and how much to intervene in markets.
questions.a: It should intervene where markets fail, such as unaffordable essentials, monopolies and public goods, and do so carefully with minimum distortion, considering the voices of consumers, producers and workers, and remaining accountable to the people.

questions.q: Vik says the government should never interfere in markets. Evaluate.
questions.a: Not entirely. Markets can be unfair, have monopolies and under-provide public goods, so some intervention is needed. But excessive intervention also has costs, so a balance is needed.

questions.q: Suggest a fair policy for bus fares in your town and say how you would balance passengers and operators.
questions.a: Set a maximum fare based on cost so passengers are protected, but allow enough to cover operators' costs and give subsidies for the poor so service continues and quality is maintained.
